pg-269-the-open-window.hook: A nervous visitor meets a self-possessed niece, who has a very particular explanation for the open window.
pg-269-the-open-window.blurb: Framton Nuttel, sent to the country to calm his nerves, pays a polite call armed with a letter of introduction. While he waits for his hostess, her fifteen-year-old niece keeps him company, and tells him why the French window stands open. A sharp, brief comedy of manners about who really controls a conversation.

pg-375-an-occurrence-at-owl-creek-bridge.hook: In wartime Alabama, a planter stands on a bridge with a rope around his neck.
pg-375-an-occurrence-at-owl-creek-bridge.blurb: In the American Civil War, a civilian is about to be hanged from a railroad bridge while a company of soldiers stands at attention. The story moves between that scene and the life that brought him there, in precise, unhurried prose. A classic of the short form, remembered for how it handles time and what a mind does under pressure.

pg-396-the-lady-or-the-tiger.hook: A semi-barbaric king settles guilt with two doors, a tiger behind one and a bride behind the other.
pg-396-the-lady-or-the-tiger.blurb: In a faraway kingdom, a king with peculiar ideas of justice stages public trials in an arena. The accused must choose between two identical doors: one hides a hungry tiger, the other a bride. When the king's own daughter loves the wrong man, the old system faces its hardest case. A famous short story about love, jealousy and chance.

pg-1063-the-cask-of-amontillado.hook: At carnival time, a man with a grudge invites a wine-lover down into his family catacombs.
pg-1063-the-cask-of-amontillado.blurb: Montresor has endured a thousand insults from Fortunato and has sworn revenge, carefully and without risk. On the night of the carnival he flatters his rival's pride in wine and leads him down into the damp vaults beneath the family palazzo. A short, chilling monologue of courtesy and cold intent, told by the avenger himself.

pg-1064-the-masque-of-the-red-death.hook: A prince seals himself and his friends inside an abbey to escape a plague, and throws a masked ball.
pg-1064-the-masque-of-the-red-death.blurb: A deadly plague has half emptied Prince Prospero's lands, so he withdraws to a fortified abbey with a thousand companions and shuts the world out. Months later he hosts a lavish masquerade in a suite of seven coloured rooms, where an ebony clock chimes the hours and the revellers try not to think about what waits beyond the walls.

pg-2148-the-tell-tale-heart.hook: A nervous narrator insists he is perfectly sane while he describes, calmly, what he did to an old man.
pg-2148-the-tell-tale-heart.blurb: He loved the old man, he says; it was only the eye, pale blue and filmed over like a vulture's. The narrator insists he is not mad, only sharper in his senses than anyone, and sets out to prove it by calmly telling how he went about his plan. A short, feverish monologue that grows louder as it goes.

pg-7256-the-gift-of-the-magi.hook: On Christmas Eve, a poor young wife has $1.87 and one idea for the perfect gift.
pg-7256-the-gift-of-the-magi.blurb: Della and Jim are young, poor and devoted, with exactly two treasures between them. With one day left before Christmas and almost no money, Della sets out to find Jim the perfect present, whatever it costs her. A warm, wry, much-loved tale of love and sacrifice, told in a teasing storyteller's voice.

pg-2814-araby.hook: A Dublin schoolboy, in love from a distance, promises to bring a girl something from the bazaar.
pg-2814-araby.blurb: On a blind street in Dublin, a boy spends his mornings watching a neighbour's door for a glimpse of his friend's sister. When she mentions a grand bazaar called Araby, he makes her a promise and counts the slow days until Saturday. A quiet, exact story of first love and the gap between imagination and the real world.

pg-2776-the-cop-and-the-anthem.hook: A New York vagrant tries everything he can think of to get himself arrested before winter arrives.
pg-2776-the-cop-and-the-anthem.blurb: Soapy, who sleeps on a park bench in Madison Square, has an annual plan for the cold months: get himself sent to jail for a winter of free board. This year, though, the police stubbornly refuse to cooperate. A gently comic tale of schemes that go wrong, with a streak of sympathy for New York's down-and-out.

pg-1080-a-modest-proposal.hook: A calm, reasonable-sounding pamphlet offers a solution to Irish poverty that no reader will forget.
pg-1080-a-modest-proposal.blurb: In 1729 Jonathan Swift wrote as a sober economist, deploying figures and projections on the plight of Ireland's poor. His narrator lays out a scheme in cool, practical language, anticipating objections and listing its advantages one by one. One of the sharpest satires in English, it still unsettles readers; be prepared for disturbing subject matter.

pg-12122-the-monkeys-paw.hook: A retired soldier leaves a shrivelled paw with a family, promising three wishes and a warning.
pg-12122-the-monkeys-paw.blurb: On a wet, windy night, the Whites welcome an old friend home from India. He carries a talisman: a dried paw said to grant three wishes to each of three owners, at a price. The family laughs it off, until the first wish is spoken. A classic of the macabre, built on a small family's ordinary hopes.

pg-1289-the-signal-man.hook: A traveller calls down to a lonely railway signalman and sees a strange look cross the man's face.
pg-1289-the-signal-man.blurb: Deep in a damp railway cutting, a signalman keeps watch beside the mouth of a tunnel. When a visitor hails him from above, the man reacts as if he has heard that very call before. Over two nights of conversation he confides what has been troubling him. A masterly Victorian ghost story, quietly told, from Dickens's Christmas writing.

pg-1952-the-yellow-wallpaper.hook: A woman is ordered to rest in a rented country house, and begins to study the wallpaper.
pg-1952-the-yellow-wallpaper.blurb: Her husband is a physician, and he has prescribed rest, fresh air and no work whatever. So the narrator keeps a secret journal in the big upstairs room of their rented summer house, noticing everything: the barred windows, the old garden, and above all the strange wallpaper. A landmark of early feminist fiction, told in short, intimate entries.

pg-3172-fenimore-coopers-literary-offenc.hook: Mark Twain takes a comic, merciless look at James Fenimore Cooper's frontier novels, rule by rule.
pg-3172-fenimore-coopers-literary-offenc.blurb: Three eminent critics had praised Cooper's novels as works of art. Mark Twain, who had read them, disagrees. He sets out rules for good storytelling and measures Deerslayer and The Pathfinder against them, with a sharp eye for broken twigs, impossible boats and impossible rifle shots. A gleeful literary demolition, funny and pointed. Includes period stereotypes.

pg-512-the-birthmark.hook: A brilliant scientist marries a beautiful woman and cannot stop looking at one small mark on her cheek.
pg-512-the-birthmark.blurb: Aylmer is a man of science, newly married to Georgiana, whose beauty is flawless except for a small crimson mark on her cheek. He cannot stop noticing it, and she begins to dread his gaze. When he offers to remove it, they withdraw to his laboratory, where his experiments grow stranger. A haunting parable of perfection, ambition and love.

pg-13415-the-lady-with-the-dog.hook: At a seaside resort, a married man notices a woman who is always seen with a small white dog.
pg-13415-the-lady-with-the-dog.blurb: Dmitri Gurov, a Moscow banker, is spending a fortnight in Yalta when he notices a young woman walking alone with her dog. What begins as a light holiday flirtation follows both of them home, to different towns and different marriages. A quiet, observant story about secrecy, middle age and a love that arrives later than expected.

pg-932-the-fall-of-the-house-of-usher.hook: Summoned by a troubled friend, a visitor arrives at a decaying mansion by a black, still lake.
pg-932-the-fall-of-the-house-of-usher.blurb: A letter begs the narrator to visit his boyhood friend Roderick Usher, who is ill in body and mind. He finds the ancient family house crumbling and gloomy, with Roderick and his ailing sister living in strange seclusion. The friends pass the days with painting, music and old books, but the house seems to press in. Poe's Gothic masterpiece.

pg-2148-the-purloined-letter.hook: A police prefect has searched a minister's house for a stolen letter; Dupin has a different approach.
pg-2148-the-purloined-letter.blurb: One gusty evening in Paris, the Prefect of Police brings the amateur detective C. Auguste Dupin a delicate problem: a letter has been stolen, the thief is known, and months of meticulous searching have found nothing. Dupin listens, smokes his pipe, and considers how people hide things and how others look for them. A detective classic built on conversation.

pg-1661-a-scandal-in-bohemia.hook: A masked client asks Sherlock Holmes to retrieve a compromising photograph before a royal wedding is announced.
pg-1661-a-scandal-in-bohemia.blurb: Dr. Watson, now married, calls on his old friend Sherlock Holmes and finds him waiting for a mysterious visitor. The masked caller claims to be a count, but his business is a royal embarrassment that could unravel a coming wedding. With three days to act, Holmes turns to disguises and stratagems. The story that introduced Irene Adler.

pg-1661-the-red-headed-league.hook: A pawnbroker with brilliant red hair is offered easy money to copy an encyclopedia. Holmes smells something odd.
pg-1661-the-red-headed-league.blurb: Jabez Wilson, a London pawnbroker with a fiery head of hair, tells Sherlock Holmes how he landed a very well-paid job for which only red-haired men may apply. The work is oddly light and the rules oddly strict, and then one morning the whole arrangement vanishes. Holmes and Watson set out to find the explanation. A comic, ingenious case.

pg-71-on-the-duty-of-civil-disobedience.hook: Why a just person might refuse to pay taxes to a government that supports slavery and war.
pg-71-on-the-duty-of-civil-disobedience.blurb: In 1849 Henry David Thoreau explains why he refused to pay his poll tax to a state that supported slavery and the Mexican War. He argues that conscience should outrank majority rule, that voting alone is not enough, and that under unjust government a just person belongs in prison. He also recounts his night in jail. A deeply influential essay.

pg-2944-compensation.hook: Emerson argues that every gain has its cost and every loss its hidden gift.
pg-2944-compensation.blurb: Emerson begins with a sermon he found unconvincing and sets out his own view of justice: in nature and in human life, every excess brings a defect and every advantage a price. He traces this balance through animals, politics, proverbs, work and friendship, and finds in it an argument for honesty. A calm, searching essay on loss, gain and character.

pg-16643-self-reliance.hook: A famous call to trust your own mind, resist conformity and be misunderstood.
pg-16643-self-reliance.blurb: Emerson urges readers to trust their own thoughts over borrowed opinions, tradition and the approval of the crowd. Moving from childhood to society, religion, travel and property, he argues that a person's character, not their possessions or their followers, is the only lasting source of strength. An energetic, quotable essay and a foundation of American individualism.

pg-512-rappaccinis-daughter.hook: A student in Padua falls for a physician's daughter, who tends a garden of strange, beautiful plants.
pg-512-rappaccinis-daughter.blurb: Giovanni Guasconti arrives in Padua to study and takes a room overlooking a walled garden, where a pale scientist works among strange, vivid plants. The scientist's daughter, Beatrice, is as radiant as her flowers. As Giovanni is drawn closer, a rival professor warns him that all is not what it seems. A feverish tale of love, science and suspicion.

pg-14522-the-canterville-ghost.hook: A wealthy American family buys an English country house, ghost included, and refuses to be frightened.
pg-14522-the-canterville-ghost.blurb: When the practical Otis family buys Canterville Chase, they brush aside every warning that it is haunted by a murderous ghost. Armed with stain remover, bottles of lubricating oil and two mischievous twins, they treat the centuries-old spirit as a household nuisance. A comic reversal of the traditional ghost story, by Oscar Wilde.

pg-36238-the-mantle.hook: A humble copying clerk in St Petersburg scrimps and saves for one thing: a warm new winter coat.
pg-36238-the-mantle.blurb: Akaki Akakievitch is a minor government clerk whose whole life is copying documents. When the St Petersburg winter exposes the ruin of his old cloak, he lives on almost nothing to afford a new one, and for a short while he is almost happy. Gogol's gentle, satirical and eventually haunting story of an overlooked man and the officials around him.

pg-2814-the-dead.hook: A Dublin Christmas party, a nervous after-dinner speech, and one old song that stirs unexpected memories.
pg-2814-the-dead.blurb: Every year the Misses Morkan hold a festive dance on Usher's Island. This year their nephew Gabriel, a writer and teacher, is nervous about his after-dinner speech and stung by a sharp exchange with a fellow guest. The evening moves through music, supper and farewells, then follows Gabriel and his wife to a hotel room. A masterpiece of quiet observation.

pg-35-the-time-machine.hook: A Victorian inventor builds a machine that travels through time and returns with an astonishing tale.
pg-35-the-time-machine.blurb: At a dinner in suburban London, a host explains the fourth dimension and shows his guests a small working model. A week later he staggers in, dishevelled and exhausted, ready to tell what happened when he tried the full-sized machine. His account reaches a distant future of surprising beauty and hidden dread. A classic of early science fiction.

pg-2147-the-oval-portrait.hook: A wounded traveller shelters in an abandoned château and finds one portrait he cannot stop looking at.
pg-2147-the-oval-portrait.blurb: In an abandoned château in the Apennines, a wounded man studies the paintings by candlelight, and a small book that describes them. One portrait holds him, and the book tells how it was made. A brief, atmospheric tale about art, devotion and what a likeness can cost.

pg-2148-the-facts-in-the-case-of-m-valde.hook: A mesmerist attempts an experiment no one has tried: putting a man into a trance at the moment of death.
pg-2148-the-facts-in-the-case-of-m-valde.blurb: Told as a sober case report, Poe's narrator describes the mesmeric trance of a dying friend and what the experiment seemed to hold back. In the cool voice of a scientific witness, a medical curiosity becomes one of the most notorious tales of the macabre.

pg-2148-the-imp-of-the-perverse.hook: A narrator argues that everyone is driven by an impulse to do exactly what they know they should not.
pg-2148-the-imp-of-the-perverse.blurb: Poe opens with a sharp little essay on perverseness, a motive that seems to have no motive, then shows what it can do to one careful man. Part philosophy, part confession, it is short, strange and hard to forget.

pg-924-to-be-read-at-dusk.hook: At a mountain convent in Switzerland, five couriers trade stories about strange things that cannot quite be explained.
pg-924-to-be-read-at-dusk.blurb: A narrator smoking on a bench at the Great St Bernard overhears five couriers arguing about ghosts. Two stories follow: a bride haunted by a dream, and two brothers parted for a night. A short, chilling frame tale from Dickens in his Christmas-ghost manner.

pg-13334-a-horseman-in-the-sky.hook: A young Virginian on sentry duty in 1861 must decide what duty demands when an enemy appears on the cliff.
pg-13334-a-horseman-in-the-sky.blurb: On a Virginia mountaintop in the Civil War, a Union soldier asleep at his post wakes to find a mounted enemy scout against the sky. Bierce, a veteran himself, tells it in four tightly built sections: a short, unflinching story about duty, conscience and one decision.

pg-13334-a-watcher-by-the-dead.hook: A doctor bets that a man cannot spend a night alone with a corpse in a locked, dark room.
pg-13334-a-watcher-by-the-dead.blurb: A late-night wager in San Francisco: could any man shut in a dark room with a dead body keep his nerve until morning? Bierce plays out the bet in four short chapters, moving between the room and the men who set it.

pg-13334-the-boarded-window.hook: A hermit in the Ohio woods lives behind a boarded window, and the narrator knows why.
pg-13334-the-boarded-window.blurb: In 1830, a silent pioneer lives alone in a log cabin whose only window has been nailed shut. The narrator, who heard the story from his grandfather, tells what happened on the night his wife died. A very short, grim tale of grief and darkness.

pg-13334-the-eyes-of-the-panther.hook: A woman refuses to marry the man she loves and finally tells him why: she says she is insane.
pg-13334-the-eyes-of-the-panther.blurb: Irene Marlowe refuses to marry Jenner Brading, and explains with a story from her family's past on the edge of the frontier. Bierce frames a night of terror inside a courtship, then lets a lawyer's theory test it. A gothic tale of love and fear.

pg-13334-the-man-and-the-snake.hook: A man reading about the snake's hypnotic gaze notices two bright points of light beneath his bed.
pg-13334-the-man-and-the-snake.blurb: Bierce sets a sceptical, comfortable gentleman and a very old superstition in one room. Harker Brayton, houseguest of a scientist who keeps reptiles, finds he cannot act as reason says he should. A short, tightly controlled story of fear and fascination.

pg-11870-the-red-room.hook: A confident young man insists no ghost can frighten him, and spends a night in a haunted castle room.
pg-11870-the-red-room.blurb: Three ancient, unfriendly caretakers warn a sceptical visitor against the red room of Lorraine Castle. He goes anyway, with a revolver and a good supply of candles. Wells builds a classic ghost story from darkness, imagination and certainty.

pg-11870-the-moth.hook: Two rival entomologists fight a bitter feud, and one of them cannot get the other out of his head.
pg-11870-the-moth.blurb: Wells turns a petty scientific quarrel into a ghost story. Hapley has spent twenty years trying to destroy Pawkins, and when his rival dies he cannot stop thinking about him, until an unknown moth appears. A sharp, darkly funny tale about obsession.

pg-42989-the-apple.hook: On his way to a first teaching post, a young man is offered a remarkable gift on the train.
pg-42989-the-apple.blurb: A stranger in a railway carriage tells an extraordinary tale of a golden fruit and asks a young schoolmaster whether he would want to know everything. Wells's gentle, wry fantasy asks what perfect knowledge might cost, and what we do when it is handed to us by accident.

pg-29220-a-haunted-house.hook: A ghostly couple wander an old house, opening doors, looking for something they left behind.
pg-29220-a-haunted-house.blurb: Virginia Woolf's brief, luminous story hovers between ghost tale and love poem. A sleeper hears a couple moving through the rooms of an old house, searching for a buried treasure, and wonders what they want. In under seven hundred words, a quiet piece about love and what lingers.
pg-29220-a-haunted-house.overrideReason: Plain, short sentences, but the dreamlike, impressionist prose asks for a practised reader.

pg-13707-dr-heideggers-experiment.hook: An eccentric old doctor invites four elderly friends to try a drink from the Fountain of Youth.
pg-13707-dr-heideggers-experiment.blurb: In his cobwebbed study, Dr. Heidegger offers four old friends the chance to be young again, and watches closely what they do with it. One of Hawthorne's best-known tales, a wry fable about experience, folly and whether anyone ever learns from the past.

pg-13707-the-ambitious-guest.hook: A traveller with great ambitions spends one September evening with a family at the foot of a mountain.
pg-13707-the-ambitious-guest.blurb: In the White Mountains, a family welcomes a young stranger to their fire, and the talk turns to ambition, memory and what each of them most wishes for. Hawthorne builds warmth and foreboding at once, and leaves a quiet question about what is remembered.

pg-13707-wakefield.hook: A London husband says he is going on a short trip, and takes lodgings in the next street.
pg-13707-wakefield.blurb: Hawthorne retells a half-remembered story: a man leaves his wife for a week, and then keeps putting off his return while living within sight of his own front door. An essayistic, unsettling study of habit, vanity and how easily a life can slip away.

pg-2814-the-sisters.hook: A boy learns an old priest he knew has died, and the adults talk around what they will not say.
pg-2814-the-sisters.blurb: The opening story of Joyce's Dubliners follows a boy through the days after the death of his old friend, a priest. In the pauses and unfinished sentences of the adults, we sense how much is left unsaid. A subtle, haunting start to a classic collection.

pg-66871-the-fly.hook: A comfortable businessman is visited by an old friend who mentions something he has long avoided thinking about.
pg-66871-the-fly.blurb: Mansfield sets an old man's chatter against the stillness of a businessman's office, then turns her attention to a fly in an inkpot. A precise, devastating story of grief, power and avoidance, written in the years after the First World War.

pg-773-the-sphinx-without-a-secret.hook: A man shows an old friend a photograph and asks whether this is the face of someone he can trust.
pg-773-the-sphinx-without-a-secret.blurb: In Paris, an English lord tells an old college friend about the beautiful, secretive woman he loved in London, and what he found out about her. Wilde's short, elegant tale is a puzzle about trust, secrecy and what we imagine when we want a mystery.

pg-13437-the-bet.hook: A banker bets two million that a young lawyer cannot endure fifteen years of solitary confinement.
pg-13437-the-bet.blurb: After an argument about capital punishment, a rich banker and a young lawyer make a wager. Chekhov follows the years of confinement and the last night before it ends, when the banker has his own reasons to be afraid. A story about money, time and what a person may come to value.

pg-1429-bank-holiday.hook: A street band plays on a hot holiday afternoon, and a crowd drifts up the hill.
pg-1429-bank-holiday.blurb: A single sunlit page of crowded street life: musicians, fortune-tellers, stalls, ice cream and a hot afternoon. Mansfield strings together glimpses of strangers like a row of snapshots. A vivid, nearly plotless sketch of a holiday crowd.

pg-1429-her-first-ball.hook: Leila, a country girl, arrives at her very first dance, certain it is the loveliest night of her life.
pg-1429-her-first-ball.blurb: Mansfield catches the dizzy excitement of a first dance, from the cab ride to the supper room. Then one partner says something unkind and true, and Leila's evening shifts. A short, quick-moving story of youth, delight and the first sense of time passing.

pg-1429-life-of-ma-parker.hook: A charwoman goes to work the day after burying her grandson, and looks for somewhere to cry.
pg-1429-life-of-ma-parker.blurb: Ma Parker, an old cleaner, comes to work the morning after her grandson's funeral, while the literary gentleman she works for fumbles for something to say. As she scrubs, her hard life comes back to her. A compassionate story about grief, class and who is allowed to break down.

pg-1429-marriage-a-la-mode.hook: Each Saturday William takes the train to see his wife Isabel, who now lives among fashionable friends.
pg-1429-marriage-a-la-mode.blurb: William loves Isabel, but since she joined a new artistic circle she seems like someone else. Mansfield follows one seaside weekend. A sharp, sorrowful comedy about modern manners, shallow cleverness and the distance that can open between husband and wife.

pg-1429-miss-brill.hook: On a sunny Sunday, Miss Brill puts on her fur and goes to hear the band in the park.
pg-1429-miss-brill.blurb: Every Sunday Miss Brill sits in the public gardens of a French town and watches the world go by, and she has come to feel part of the show. Mansfield's much-loved story is quiet and precise, about loneliness and imagination.

pg-1429-mr-and-mrs-dove.hook: On his last afternoon in England, a shy young man goes to ask the girl he loves a question.
pg-1429-mr-and-mrs-dove.blurb: Reggie is about to leave for Rhodesia, with a nervous plan, a checked tie and a long list of reasons why he has no chance. Anne laughs every time she sees him, and doesn't know why. A gentle comedy of a proposal, about shyness, love and a pair of doves.

pg-1429-the-singing-lesson.hook: A schoolteacher takes her singing class on the morning a letter from her fiancé breaks her heart.
pg-1429-the-singing-lesson.blurb: Miss Meadows conducts a girls' singing class with cold fury, while a letter from her fiancé plays over and over in her head. Mansfield sets the school's sentimental songs against her private despair. A short, brisk, wickedly funny story.

pg-1429-the-voyage.hook: A girl in mourning crosses the strait on a night boat with her grandmother, towards a new home.
pg-1429-the-voyage.blurb: Fenella, dressed in black, boards the Picton boat with her grandmother and says goodbye to her father on a dark wharf. Mansfield follows one night's crossing in small, exact details: a tender, quietly sad story about loss, change and the strange comfort of an old woman's routines.

pg-44385-a-dill-pickle.hook: After six years, two former lovers meet again over coffee in a London café.
pg-44385-a-dill-pickle.blurb: Vera and the man she once loved talk of travel, music and the past, each hearing something different in the same words. Mansfield listens closely to what is said and what is not, in a story about memory, vanity and how two people can remember one afternoon in opposite ways.

pg-44385-pictures.hook: Out-of-work singer Miss Moss spends a Saturday going from one theatrical agent to the next, hungry and nearly broke.
pg-44385-pictures.blurb: Miss Ada Moss, a stout, out-of-work contralto in postwar London, goes from agent to agent looking for a part and a meal, while her landlady wants the rent by eight o'clock. Mansfield mixes comedy with a hard look at poverty and pride, in a day that darkens as it goes.

pg-44385-sun-and-moon.hook: Two small children watch a grand dinner party being prepared, and one of them is struck by the ice pudding.
pg-44385-sun-and-moon.blurb: Seen through the eyes of two small children, Sun and Moon, a house prepares for a party, with its flowers, hired chairs and a miraculous ice pudding. Mansfield catches the wonder of the preparations, and a child's bewilderment at what grown-ups do with beautiful things.

pg-66871-a-cup-of-tea.hook: A rich young woman invites a hungry stranger home for tea, as an adventure.
pg-66871-a-cup-of-tea.blurb: Rosemary Fell has everything, including a taste for grand gestures. When a girl in the street begs her for tea money, she decides to be generous. Mansfield's polished social comedy looks at charity and vanity, and at how kindness can depend on its audience.

pg-66871-the-dolls-house.hook: A magnificent doll's house arrives at the Burnell home, and every girl at school wants to see it.
pg-66871-the-dolls-house.blurb: The Burnell girls' new doll's house is the talk of the school, but the washerwoman's daughters are never invited. Mansfield draws on a New Zealand childhood to show how snobbery is taught. A short, precise story about class.

pg-160-a-pair-of-silk-stockings.hook: A poor mother with fifteen dollars in her purse finds herself buying something for herself.
pg-160-a-pair-of-silk-stockings.blurb: Mrs. Sommers has fifteen dollars and a household of children to clothe. Chopin follows one afternoon of shopping in which a mother, tired of thrift, does something she never planned. A short, sympathetic study of desire, self-denial and the small luxuries that can feel like freedom.

pg-160-a-respectable-woman.hook: A woman dislikes her husband's quiet houseguest, and finds she cannot explain why.
pg-160-a-respectable-woman.blurb: Mrs. Baroda is annoyed that her husband's friend Gouvernail is coming to stay on their Louisiana plantation. Then he arrives. Chopin's brief, witty story of attraction and restraint turns on a single evening.

pg-160-the-kiss.hook: A calculating young woman is caught in one man's arms while another sits in the shadows.
pg-160-the-kiss.blurb: Nathalie has decided to marry a rich man, until an unexpected kiss threatens the plan. Chopin shows in a few pages how quickly a clever woman can arrange a scene to suit herself. A brisk, ironic story about love, money and calculation.

pg-63025-regret.hook: A self-reliant Louisiana farm owner is left in charge of her neighbour's four children for two weeks.
pg-63025-regret.blurb: Mamzelle Aurélie has lived alone and contentedly for fifty years, until four children are left on her porch. Chopin shows a Louisiana woman discovering what she did not know she was missing. A short, tender story about independence and an unexpected visit.

pg-2814-eveline.hook: On the evening she plans to leave home with a sailor, Eveline sits at her window and weighs her life.
pg-2814-eveline.blurb: Eveline has promised to leave Dublin with Frank, and tonight she must decide. Joyce moves between her hard present, her childhood and a promise to her dead mother. A short, intense story about duty, fear and the pull of escape, among the most quietly powerful in Dubliners.

pg-2814-the-boarding-house.hook: A boarding-house landlady has decided how her daughter's affair with one of her lodgers must end.
pg-2814-the-boarding-house.blurb: Mrs. Mooney runs her Dublin boarding house the way her father ran his butcher's shop, and she has decided what must happen between her daughter Polly and Mr. Doran. Joyce lets us into all three minds in turn. A sharp, economical comedy of respectability and pressure.

pg-2814-a-painful-case.hook: A precise, solitary Dublin bank clerk forms an unusual friendship.
pg-2814-a-painful-case.blurb: Mr. Duffy lives by order and distance until he meets Mrs. Sinico at a concert. Joyce traces a friendship, a decision and its consequences in cool, exact prose. One of the great portraits of loneliness in Dubliners, about what a person chooses not to feel.

pg-2814-an-encounter.hook: Two schoolboys skip school for a day of adventure by the Dublin docks, and meet a stranger in a field.
pg-2814-an-encounter.blurb: Boys raised on Wild West stories skip school to look for a real adventure in the streets and docks of Dublin. They find something else. Joyce tells it through a narrator's memory of excitement, boredom and unease: a short, unsettling story of childhood and an unwelcome adult world.

pg-2814-clay.hook: Maria, a tiny, tidy laundry worker, spends Hallow Eve with the family she once helped to raise.
pg-2814-clay.blurb: Everyone at the laundry is fond of Maria, and tonight she is visiting Joe's family with cakes in her bag. Joyce follows her from tram to party with tender, ironic attention. A small story about kindness, loneliness and what a person is able to see of her own life.

pg-1444-one-thousand-dollars.hook: Bobby Gillian inherits exactly one thousand dollars, and must report to his uncle's lawyers how he spends it.
pg-1444-one-thousand-dollars.blurb: A rich young idler is left an awkward sum in his uncle's will, with one condition: he must account for how he spends it. He asks his friend Old Bryson how a man should spend it, and gets plenty of answers. A brisk New York comedy of money and habit.

pg-1646-a-retrieved-reformation.hook: Safecracker Jimmy Valentine is pardoned, and a detective who knows his methods waits for the next robbery.
pg-1646-a-retrieved-reformation.blurb: Jimmy Valentine leaves prison early, insisting he never cracked a safe in his life. Soon a run of neat robberies turns up across the Midwest, and detective Ben Price recognises the work. O. Henry's famous story follows a clever thief and the man on his trail.

pg-2776-after-twenty-years.hook: A patrolman on his night beat meets a man in a doorway, keeping an appointment made long ago.
pg-2776-after-twenty-years.blurb: Two boyhood friends agreed to meet at a restaurant door in New York in twenty years, whatever had become of them. Tonight is the night, and one of them has come a thousand miles to keep the promise. A very short story about friendship and the long time between meetings.

pg-2776-mammon-and-the-archer.hook: A retired soap king believes money can buy anything, and his son says there is one thing it cannot.
pg-2776-mammon-and-the-archer.blurb: Anthony Rockwall made millions in soap and trusts money above everything. His son Richard is in love with a girl who sails for Europe in two days, and has one short cab ride in which to speak to her. A light New York comedy of a father and a son.
pg-2776-mammon-and-the-archer.overrideReason: Brisk sentences carry period slang and wordplay that a younger reader would miss.

pg-2776-springtime-a-la-carte.hook: A New York typist pays for her meals by typing a restaurant's daily menus, and the calendar says spring.
pg-2776-springtime-a-la-carte.blurb: Sarah lives on odd typing jobs and one good bargain: a neat new menu every day for Schulenberg's Home Restaurant, in return for three meals. Winter will not let go, though the almanac claims it is spring. O. Henry opens with mock advice on how not to begin a story..

pg-2776-the-furnished-room.hook: A young man searching for a lost love rents a shabby furnished room on New York's West Side.
pg-2776-the-furnished-room.blurb: For five months he has asked in theatres and boarding houses for one girl, Eloise Vashner. Tonight he rings his twelfth doorbell and takes a room from a housekeeper who cannot remember any of her lodgers. O. Henry opens on a district of rented rooms where thousands have lived and none have stayed.
pg-2776-the-furnished-room.overrideReason: Short sentences hide dense, period vocabulary and a layered scene of rented rooms.

pg-2776-the-green-door.hook: A piano salesman who loves adventure is handed a card bearing three handwritten words: The Green Door.
pg-2776-the-green-door.blurb: Rudolf Steiner follows every strange invitation the city offers. One evening a card is pressed into his hand with three words written on it, and he cannot rest until he finds out what they mean. A playful O. Henry tale about the spirit of adventure.

pg-2776-the-romance-of-a-busy-broker.hook: On a frantic morning at a New York brokerage, Harvey Maxwell has time for nothing but the ticker.
pg-2776-the-romance-of-a-busy-broker.blurb: Harvey Maxwell lives by the ticker, and today the market is wild. His stenographer, Miss Leslie, arrives softly radiant and asks the confidential clerk an odd question about replacing her. A very short comedy about a man with no time and a day with too much in it.

pg-2776-the-skylight-room.hook: A landlady shows rooms in order of price, and the cheapest is a closet at the top of the house.
pg-2776-the-skylight-room.blurb: Mrs. Parker shows every room-hunter her better rooms first, until poverty is plain. Miss Leeson, a very small, cheerful typist, ends up in the Skylight Room, seven feet by eight, and soon wins the roomers on the front steps. O. Henry's gently comic story of a boarding house and the people on its stoop.
pg-2776-the-skylight-room.overrideReason: Short sentences and plain words, but the humour and boarding-house slang need an experienced reader.

pg-3707-the-last-leaf.hook: Two young artists share a Greenwich Village studio, and in November one of them falls ill with pneumonia.
pg-3707-the-last-leaf.blurb: Sue and Johnsy, from Maine and California, share a studio at the top of a Greenwich Village house. When pneumonia strikes Johnsy, the doctor says her only chance is to want to live, and she begins counting the leaves falling outside her window. A story of friendship and illness.

pg-3077-two-friends.hook: In besieged Paris, two fishing friends meet by chance and decide to try for their old river bank.
pg-3077-two-friends.blurb: Paris is starving under siege. Two friends who used to fish every Sunday meet on the boulevard, drink absinthe on empty stomachs, and wonder whether they could pass the lines to their favourite stretch of the Seine. A story of friendship and war, told in plain, even prose.

pg-12732-the-piece-of-string.hook: A thrifty Norman peasant picks up a piece of string on market day, and an old rival sees him.
pg-12732-the-piece-of-string.blurb: At Goderville market, Master Hauchecorne picks up a bit of string, and the harness-maker he once quarrelled with is watching. Later a wallet is reported lost on the same road, and the gendarmes send for him. Maupassant's sharp portrait of Norman village life.

pg-12758-the-necklace.hook: A clerk's pretty wife, who longs for a richer life, is invited to a grand ministry ball.
pg-12758-the-necklace.blurb: Mathilde Loisel believes she was born for luxury, and she hates her small flat and plain dinners. When her husband brings home an invitation to a ball at the Ministry, she has nothing to wear and no jewels. A classic French story about a woman who wants more than she has.

pg-773-the-model-millionaire.hook: Charming, penniless Hughie Erskine loves Laura Merton, but her father wants ten thousand pounds first.
pg-773-the-model-millionaire.blurb: Hughie Erskine has good looks, good manners and no money, which is why Colonel Merton will not hear of an engagement. Calling on his painter friend Alan Trevor one morning, Hughie finds him at work on a life-size picture of a ragged old beggar. A light Wilde comedy of love, money and an artist's studio.

pg-7239-a-dark-brown-dog.hook: A small boy meets a stray dog on a street corner, and the dog is quick to make friends.
pg-7239-a-dark-brown-dog.blurb: On a sunny street corner, a child strikes a friendly little dog that has wandered up to him, and the dog answers with apology. Stephen Crane follows the pair home to a tenement. A short, plain-spoken story told mostly from the dog's side.

pg-6373-the-luck-of-roaring-camp.hook: In 1850, an all-male mining camp gathers outside a cabin where the camp's only woman is giving birth.
pg-6373-the-luck-of-roaring-camp.blurb: A hundred hard-bitten miners wait outside a cabin in the Sierra foothills. Nobody in Roaring Camp has ever seen a birth, and the hat is passed for the newcomer. Bret Harte's best-known story asks what a camp of gamblers and outlaws will do with a baby.

pg-56870-twenty-six-of-us-and-one-other.hook: Twenty-six bakers work in a damp cellar, and the one bright moment of their day is the girl upstairs.
pg-56870-twenty-six-of-us-and-one-other.blurb: Twenty-six men knead dough from dawn until late at night in a basement under a bakery, poorly paid and closely watched. Each morning a girl from the embroidery workshop upstairs comes to the little window for hot biscuits, and for the men she is the nearest thing to sunshine. Told by one of them, in the voice of "we".

pg-23344-the-magic-fishbone.hook: A king with nineteen children buys some salmon, and an irritable fairy gives him a message about a fishbone.
pg-23344-the-magic-fishbone.blurb: King Watkins is short of money, and his many children are outgrowing their clothes. On the way to his office he meets the Good Fairy Grandmarina, who is full of instructions and will not be asked why. Dickens writes as a seven-year-old girl, in a funny, affectionate fairy tale about a magic present that can be used only once.

pg-456-the-diamond-maker.hook: On the Embankment at night, a ragged stranger tells a passer-by he makes diamonds, and offers him one.
pg-456-the-diamond-maker.blurb: A tired Londoner lingers by the river after dark when a pinched, shabby man starts a conversation. The stranger takes a large brown stone from a bag round his neck, says he made it himself, and asks a hundred pounds for it. The narrator is not rich, and must decide whether to believe him.

pg-1732-misery.hook: A sledge-driver in the snow wants to tell his passengers that his son died this week.
pg-1732-misery.blurb: Iona Potapov sits white with snow on his sledge, waiting for custom. When an officer climbs aboard he tries to say that his son has just died, but the officer wants only to be driven. A noisy trio of young men are the next fare.

pg-1944-the-huntsman.hook: In the heat of midday, a huntsman is stopped on a forest road by the wife he rarely visits.
pg-1944-the-huntsman.blurb: Yegor Vlassitch, vain of being the best shot around, strolls home from the hunt with a blackcock in his bag when a pale woman with a sickle appears at his side. She is Pelagea, his wife, who has been waiting for him since Easter. They sit down in the heat to talk.

pg-11870-the-obliterated-man.hook: A shy man who has never seen a play is made the dramatic critic of a London paper.
pg-11870-the-obliterated-man.blurb: Egbert Craddock Cummins, a quiet young man engaged to a girl who reads at the British Museum, is cornered on a staircase by his editor and handed tickets to three plays. He has never set foot in a theatre. His first night there fills him with wonder and a column of indignation.
pg-11870-the-obliterated-man.overrideReason: Short sentences, but the comic voice leans on theatre slang, literary in-jokes and period allusions.

pg-11870-the-stolen-bacillus.hook: A bacteriologist gives a curious visitor a tour of his laboratory, and a lecture on cholera.
pg-11870-the-stolen-bacillus.blurb: A bacteriologist shows a pale, nervous visitor round his laboratory: stained slides under the microscope, and sealed tubes of living disease. The visitor is keen to learn what a single broken tube could do to a city if it reached the water supply. The bacteriologist, pleased with his audience, obliges.

pg-11870-the-treasure-in-the-forest.hook: Two exhausted men paddle toward an island with a worn map that marks where treasure lies buried.
pg-11870-the-treasure-in-the-forest.blurb: Evans and Hooker, short of water and out of luck, bring a canoe through the reef towards a green island. They carry a creased map, marked in Chinese, of where a Spanish ship's treasure was hidden two centuries ago. Beyond the beach, in line with the palms, lies the hoard. First they need fresh water.

pg-12750-a-deal-in-ostriches.hook: Aboard a ship, a passenger's diamond is swallowed by one of five ostriches, and nobody knows which.
pg-12750-a-deal-in-ostriches.blurb: The taxidermist recalls a voyage on which a wealthy passenger, Sir Mohini Padishah, lost the diamond from his turban to a passing ostrich. Five birds were on board, none marked, and their keeper would hear of no stomach-pump. The passengers argue over law and ownership while the owner begins to make offers.

pg-12750-the-triumphs-of-a-taxidermist.hook: Over whisky, a taxidermist boasts to a friend about the secrets of his trade.
pg-12750-the-triumphs-of-a-taxidermist.blurb: In his cluttered den, a taxidermist, a few glasses of whisky in, feels like talking. He tells his friend Bellows what can be done with skins, glass eyes and feathers, and what collectors will pay for the result. He has begun to speak of what taxidermy might become.

pg-13409-the-looking-glass.hook: On New Year's Eve, a landowner's daughter sits alone before a looking-glass, waiting to see the man she will marry.
pg-13409-the-looking-glass.blurb: Nellie, young and pretty, thinks of nothing but marriage. On New Year's Eve she sits alone and stares into a looking-glass until the room dissolves into grey mist. A face begins to take shape in it: the man she is destined to marry. She sees their life together begin to unfold.

pg-13414-a-joke.hook: A young man takes a frightened girl tobogganing down an ice hill, and whispers into the wind.
pg-13414-a-joke.blurb: On a bright winter day, Nadenka is too afraid to ride a sledge down the ice hill, but the narrator coaxes her into it. As they fly down, he says four words, and she cannot tell whether he spoke them or the wind did. At the bottom, she asks to go again.

pg-13414-fat-and-thin.hook: Two school friends, one fat and one thin, meet by chance at a railway station and embrace.
pg-13414-fat-and-thin.blurb: At the Nikolaevsky station, a thin man with a wife, a schoolboy son and an armful of luggage recognises a fat man who has just dined. They were boys together, and they kiss three times. The thin man introduces his family and asks his old friend what he has made of himself.

pg-13414-the-death-of-a-government-clerk.hook: At the theatre, a clerk sneezes and spatters the general sitting in front of him.
pg-13414-the-death-of-a-government-clerk.blurb: Ivan Tchervyakov is enjoying an operetta from the stalls until a sneeze goes astray. The old gentleman in front of him turns out to be a civilian general from another department. Tchervyakov whispers an apology and is waved off, but cannot settle in his seat.

pg-13416-anyuta.hook: A medical student cramming anatomy asks the woman who shares his room to let him practise on her.
pg-13416-anyuta.blurb: Klotchkov, a third-year medical student in a cheap furnished room, paces about learning anatomy while Anyuta, who lives with him, embroiders a shirt collar to pay for their tea. To fix the ribs in his mind, he has her take off her blouse and marks them on her with crayon. She sits very still in the cold.

pg-13417-a-chameleon.hook: In a market square, a police superintendent must rule on a dog that has bitten a goldsmith's finger.
pg-13417-a-chameleon.blurb: Otchumyelov is crossing the market square in his new overcoat when a yelp and a shout draw him to a crowd. Hryukin the goldsmith holds up a bleeding finger, and a white puppy sits trembling. The superintendent demands to know whose dog it is, and the onlookers offer their guesses.

pg-13437-vanka.hook: On Christmas Eve, a nine-year-old apprentice sneaks ink and a pen so he can write to his grandfather.
pg-13437-vanka.blurb: Vanka Zhukov, nine, has spent three months as a shoemaker's apprentice in Moscow. While his master and mistress are at church, he kneels over a crumpled sheet and begins a letter to his grandfather in the village, picturing the old man at his post. He has a great deal to tell him.

pg-29220-kew-gardens.hook: In July, couples and strangers drift past an oval flower-bed at Kew while a snail crosses the soil.
pg-29220-kew-gardens.blurb: A hot July day at Kew. Light from an oval flower-bed falls on a snail, and a procession of strangers passes: a husband recalling an old proposal beside his wife, a man who talks to the spirits of the dead, two women trading gossip. The sketch is made of what they say as they go by.

pg-29220-the-mark-on-the-wall.hook: Sitting by the fire, someone notices a small dark mark on the wall and wonders what made it.
pg-29220-the-mark-on-the-wall.blurb: In the middle of January, with tea just finished, the narrator looks up and sees a round black mark above the mantelpiece. Is it a nail, a hole, a rose-leaf? Getting up to look seems too much trouble, so the narrator sits still, and the question leads to old houses, lost belongings and idle guesses.

pg-61-the-communist-manifesto.hook: In 1848, two writers set out a movement’s views and aims for all of Europe to read.
pg-61-the-communist-manifesto.blurb: Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels wrote this pamphlet for a small association of communists; it became one of the most influential political texts ever printed. It argues that every society has been shaped by class struggle, and that the middle class and the working class now face each other. How did the middle class rise?

pg-132-chapter-i-laying-plans.hook: An ancient military treatise opens with five factors a commander must weigh before going to war.
pg-132-chapter-i-laying-plans.blurb: Sun Tzu opens The Art of War by explaining why a state cannot neglect war, which can bring it safety or ruin. He names the five factors a commander must weigh: the moral law, heaven, earth, the commander, and method and discipline. The translator’s notes quote Chinese commentators. What does a general need to know before the first move?

pg-132-chapter-iii-attack-by-stratagem.hook: Why does an ancient general rank the siege of a walled city as the weakest course of all?
pg-132-chapter-iii-attack-by-stratagem.blurb: Sun Tzu ranks the ways of making war from best to worst, and puts the siege of a walled city last. He counts the months of preparation a siege demands, and what happens when an impatient general throws his men at the walls. The translator’s notes add examples. Is there anything better than winning a fight?

pg-132-chapter-vi-weak-points-and-strong.hook: Sun Tzu says the army that waits in the field arrives fresh, and the one that hurries arrives worn out.
pg-132-chapter-vi-weak-points-and-strong.blurb: Sun Tzu advises seizing the initiative: reach the field first, march where the enemy is not, and strike only where the defence is weak. He praises subtlety and secrecy, and the translator’s notes cite commentators and later generals. How can a force stay hidden and still command the field?

pg-147-of-the-origin-and-design-of-gover.hook: Paine begins with a few settlers in an empty land and asks why anyone needs a government.
pg-147-of-the-origin-and-design-of-gover.blurb: Thomas Paine separates society, which he says springs from our wants, from government, which he says springs from our wickedness. He pictures a handful of settlers in a new country and asks how they would organise themselves as their numbers grow. Written for ordinary colonists, it puts a plain question: what is government for?

pg-147-thoughts-on-the-present-state-of-.hook: The first shots have been fired, and Paine tells colonists the old case for reconciliation is used up.
pg-147-thoughts-on-the-present-state-of-.blurb: Paine writes after the first fighting with British troops. He takes up the claims that Britain protects the colonies and is their parent country, and asks what America gains from the link. Aimed at ordinary readers, it is a plain-spoken case made in a hurry. Does the connection with Britain help the colonies or hold them back?

pg-205-where-i-lived-and-what-i-lived-fo.hook: Thoreau “buys” every farm nearby in his imagination, then moves into a bare cabin by a pond.
pg-205-where-i-lived-and-what-i-lived-fo.blurb: Thoreau starts with the farms he has bought only in his head, and the Hollowell place he nearly bought in fact. He then describes his first days in an unfinished house on the shore of Walden Pond, near Concord, with birds and a view across the water for neighbours. What does he hope to find there?

pg-205-reading.hook: Thoreau keeps the Iliad on his table all summer and asks what it takes to read a book well.
pg-205-reading.blurb: Thoreau, in his house by the pond, keeps Homer on the table while he builds and hoes beans. He argues that reading the great books properly takes the training of an athlete, and that written language is a different thing from everyday speech. Why should reading be treated as work for a whole life?

pg-205-solitude.hook: Walking home at dusk, Thoreau finds that unseen visitors have left small gifts at his door.
pg-205-solitude.blurb: On a still evening by the pond, Thoreau comes home to find that visitors have left small signs of their calls. He describes the wide, quiet land around his house, and the single hour, early on, when he doubted that he could be happy so far from other people. Is it possible to feel at home in solitude?

pg-216-the-tao-teh-king.hook: A short book that opens by saying the Way that can be spoken of is not the true Way.
pg-216-the-tao-teh-king.blurb: Attributed to Lao-Tse, the Tao Teh King is a classic of Chinese thought, here in James Legge’s English translation. Its short chapters speak of the Tao, the Way behind all things, and of a ruler who governs by doing little. Water, the empty vessel and the valley are its images. What does it mean to act without forcing?
pg-216-the-tao-teh-king.overrideReason: The numbered clauses inflate the sentence count; the sentences are long, abstract and paradoxical.

pg-368-acres-of-diamonds.hook: A lecture opens with an Arab guide’s story of a farmer who leaves home to search for diamonds.
pg-368-acres-of-diamonds.blurb: Russell Conwell’s best-known lecture begins with a story. He retells a guide’s story of a Persian farmer who sells his land to hunt for diamonds, and sets beside it tales of a California ranch, a Pennsylvania farm and a Massachusetts mining student. His message to his Philadelphia listeners: opportunity may be close at hand. Where is it?

pg-408-i-of-our-spiritual-strivings.hook: Du Bois opens his book with the question white Americans circle round: what is it like to be a problem?
pg-408-i-of-our-spiritual-strivings.blurb: W. E. B. Du Bois begins The Souls of Black Folk with the question people hesitate to ask him. He recalls the day in childhood when he first knew he was set apart, and describes the “double-consciousness” of being both an American and a Negro. What does it cost to see yourself through other people’s eyes?

pg-408-xi-of-the-passing-of-the-first-bo.hook: A yellow slip of paper announces the birth of his son, and a father hurries home.
pg-408-xi-of-the-passing-of-the-first-bo.blurb: W. E. B. Du Bois writes of the birth of his first son: the news by telegram, the rush home, the newborn he does not at first know how to love. As the baby grows, his parents give him their whole attention, and his father thinks of the colour line that will fall across the boy’s life.

pg-408-xiii-of-the-coming-of-john.hook: In a Georgia town, two boys named John, one Black and one white, leave for school in the North.
pg-408-xiii-of-the-coming-of-john.blurb: In a small Georgia town, a Black family and a white judge each wait for a son named John, away at school in the North. At the Institute, John Jones is clumsy, cheerful and often late, and his teachers suspend him. He returns more serious, and begins to notice the colour line. Where will he take what he has learned?

pg-408-xiv-of-the-sorrow-songs.hook: Du Bois traces the songs of the enslaved and the student singers who carried them across the world.
pg-408-xiv-of-the-sorrow-songs.blurb: In the last chapter of The Souls of Black Folk, Du Bois explains the “sorrow songs” whose lines open each of its chapters. He tells how the Fisk Jubilee Singers, a small troupe on tour, carried them to the world’s stages and raised money to found a university. What do these songs say about the people who made them?

pg-1232-chapter-xvii-concerning-cruelty-.hook: Machiavelli asks whether a prince should wish to be thought merciful or cruel.
pg-1232-chapter-xvii-concerning-cruelty-.blurb: Machiavelli asks whether a prince should wish to be thought merciful or cruel, and offers Cesare Borgia and the people of Florence as his first examples. Then he poses the question the chapter is known for: whether affection or dread makes a ruler safer. Which is the safer course for a new prince?

pg-1232-chapter-xviii-concerning-the-way.hook: Machiavelli asks whether a prince should keep his word, and offers the fox and the lion.
pg-1232-chapter-xviii-concerning-the-way.blurb: Machiavelli asks whether a prince should keep his word. Rulers with great deeds to their name, he notes, have often held faith cheap, and there are two ways of contending, by law and by force, the second proper to beasts. A footnote records the offence it caused. Must a ruler keep a promise that no longer serves him?

pg-1232-chapter-xxv-what-fortune-can-eff.hook: Machiavelli takes up the old belief that fortune and God govern everything, leaving no room for skill.
pg-1232-chapter-xxv-what-fortune-can-eff.blurb: Machiavelli takes up the old belief that fortune and God govern human affairs, leaving no room for wisdom. He half grants it, allows fortune about half of our actions, and compares her to a flooding river that men can prepare for with defences. He looks at Italy as an unprotected plain. How much of life can a person steer?

pg-1656-apology.hook: At seventy, Socrates stands before a jury of Athenians accused of corrupting the young and not honouring the gods.
pg-1656-apology.blurb: Plato’s account of the speech Socrates gave at his trial in Athens. Accused of corrupting young men and neglecting the city’s gods, he answers an old slander, tells how an oracle sent him to question the city’s reputed wise men, and cross-examines his accuser Meletus. In Benjamin Jowett’s translation. How does one defend a life spent questioning others?

pg-2376-chapter-i-a-slave-among-slaves.hook: Booker T. Washington recalls his earliest years in a Virginia slave cabin, unsure of the day he was born.
pg-2376-chapter-i-a-slave-among-slaves.blurb: Booker T. Washington begins his autobiography with his birth into slavery on a Virginia plantation, in a dirt-floored cabin shared with his mother, brother and sister. He recalls hunger, rough clothing and a lonely road to the mill, and how news of the war reached the quarters. What was it like to grow up hearing whispered talk of freedom?

pg-2376-chapter-xiv-the-atlanta-expositi.hook: Washington is invited to speak for his race as the Atlanta Exposition opens.
pg-2376-chapter-xiv-the-atlanta-expositi.blurb: Booker T. Washington sets down the speech he gave at the Atlanta Exposition before a large crowd. He tells the parable of a ship crying for water while floating on fresh, and urges both races to lower their buckets where they stand, in farming, trade and service. What did he ask of each race?

pg-2680-the-second-book.hook: A Roman emperor reminds himself, in private notes, that his time is limited and each act might be his last.
pg-2680-the-second-book.blurb: Marcus Aurelius, Roman emperor, wrote these private notes to himself, here in an early English translation. Book Two begins by telling himself that his time is limited and that each act should be done as though it were the last. It turns to what should and should not trouble him. How should anyone use the time they have?

pg-2680-the-fourth-book.hook: In private notes, a Roman emperor tells himself he can always retire into his own mind for rest.
pg-2680-the-fourth-book.blurb: Marcus Aurelius keeps advising himself. People seek retreats in the country or by the sea, he says, when a retreat is always available in the mind. He reasons that all people share reason and so belong to one city, and he keeps returning to how brief life and fame are. What would make him free of distraction?

pg-2680-the-sixth-book.hook: A Roman emperor writes that the best answer to people who wrong us is not to resemble them.
pg-2680-the-sixth-book.blurb: In Book Six, Marcus Aurelius asks whether the universe is ordered or random, and how to live either way. He notes that fine food and rich wine are, looked at plainly, only fish, bird and grape juice, and that praise is only noise. Short sections, each a reminder to himself. What is worth caring about, if not these?

pg-4507-as-a-man-thinketh.hook: A little book of 1903 holds that a person’s character is the sum of their thoughts.
pg-4507-as-a-man-thinketh.blurb: James Allen’s short essay, first published in 1903, argues that people become what they habitually think. Its first chapter says character grows from thought as a plant grows from a seed, and the next likens the mind to a garden that can be tended or left to weeds. Can a person change a life by changing a habit of thought?

pg-5827-chapter-i-appearance-and-reality.hook: Bertrand Russell asks how certain anything is, starting with the colour of an ordinary table.
pg-5827-chapter-i-appearance-and-reality.blurb: Bertrand Russell begins his introduction to philosophy by asking whether any knowledge is certain enough that no reasonable person could doubt it. He studies an ordinary table, which looks different in colour, texture and shape from every angle, and asks what the “real” table could be. How much can the senses tell us?

pg-5827-chapter-xv-the-value-of-philosop.hook: Russell asks whether philosophy is just idle hair-splitting.
pg-5827-chapter-xv-the-value-of-philosop.blurb: In the closing chapter of The Problems of Philosophy, Bertrand Russell takes up the charge that philosophy is idle trifling, and answers that its value lies in what it does for the mind. He admits it has settled few questions, because the ones it can answer become sciences. Is a field of unanswered questions worth studying?

pg-11224-chapter-ii-what-utilitarianism-.hook: Mill explains what utility really means, and asks whether a human being could be content with a pig’s pleasures.
pg-11224-chapter-ii-what-utilitarianism-.blurb: John Stuart Mill defends the principle that actions are right as they promote happiness. He first clears away a misunderstanding of the word “utility”, then meets the old charge that this makes life a pursuit fit only for swine. His reply is that pleasures differ in quality as well as amount. Who is qualified to judge?

pg-34901-chapter-ii-of-the-liberty-of-th.hook: Mill considers what would be lost if one dissenting opinion were silenced by everyone else.
pg-34901-chapter-ii-of-the-liberty-of-th.blurb: Mill asks whether anyone may be stopped from voicing an opinion, even if the whole of society disagrees. He argues that silencing a view robs the human race, and turns to the cases of Socrates and the Emperor Marcus Aurelius, and to the claim that truth always survives persecution. What follows if an unpopular opinion is true?

pg-58585-the-prophet.hook: After years in a foreign city, a prophet is about to sail home when the people ask him to speak.
pg-58585-the-prophet.blurb: On the day his ship comes in, Almustafa leaves the hill above Orphalese, uneasy at what he must leave behind. The townspeople crowd round and beg him not to go. A seeress, Almitra, asks him to speak first about love, then marriage, children, giving and work. Kahlil Gibran’s 1923 book of prose poems. What will he say before he sails?
